title: How Radiation Sickness Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain acute radiation sickness: how ionizing radiation (alpha, beta, gamma) damages atoms, molecules and cells; the difference between radiation and contamination; background dose and sievert thresholds; symptoms, latent period, and bone marrow and gut damage. They discuss treatments (decontamination, Prussian blue, DTPA, transfusions, transplants), dental X-ray habits, and historical cases: Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Chernobyl, the Demon core deaths (Harry Daghlian and Louis Slotin), and the Goiânia caesium-137 accident in Brazil. The episode ends with a listener email about physician suicide and the documentary Do No Harm.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show's name and tangents, talk about Andy Kaufman and Sacha Baron Cohen, and lead into radiation sickness.

segments.title: Ionizing vs non-ionizing radiation
segments.summary: Sunlight, microwaves and cell phones are non-ionizing, so they do not cause radiation sickness. Radiation sickness requires a huge immediate dose of ionizing radiation, with symptoms such as vomiting, diarrhea and scarring.

segments.title: Alpha, beta and gamma particles
segments.summary: The three kinds of ionizing radiation are described. Alpha particles are stopped by clothing but are dangerous if inhaled or ingested, beta particles pass through clothing and can be blocked by solid objects, and gamma rays pass through most things. Ionization damages molecules and cells.

segments.title: Radiation versus contamination and X-rays
segments.summary: Contamination means radioactive material is on or in the body and can spread to others. Irradiation, such as a chest X-ray, ends when the machine is turned off. The hosts discuss dental X-rays and upselling.

segments.title: Sieverts, background dose and dose thresholds
segments.summary: The sievert measures dose. Average background exposure is about 3.6 millisieverts per year. Around 0.75 sieverts causes sickness, 3 sieverts needs medical attention, and about 10 sieverts is fatal. Survival odds depend on dose, exposed body part, and health.

segments.title: Symptoms, latent period and bone marrow damage
segments.summary: Symptoms include nausea, diarrhea, headache, fever, unconsciousness and burns. After a latent period, damage shows up as multi-organ failure, with bone marrow and gut lining especially vulnerable, leading to infection and anemia.

segments.title: Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings
segments.summary: Little Boy and Fat Man bombings are summarized, with only a few pounds of fuel undergoing fission in each, and the casualty estimates. The hosts recommend the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum.

segments.title: Chernobyl disaster
segments.summary: The 1986 Chernobyl reactor explosion is described as preventable, caused by a reactor design flaw and a safety test that removed controls. Eight died immediately, contamination covered a large area, and about 7,000 thyroid cancer cases were recorded by 2005. The sarcophagus is mentioned, along with wildlife returning to the exclusion zone.

segments.title: Demon core and Goiânia accidents
segments.summary: Harry Daghlian and Louis Slotin died after criticality accidents with the Demon core plutonium core. In Goiânia, Brazil, scavengers opened an abandoned radiotherapy unit, spread caesium-137 among people who handled it, and four people died.

segments.title: Treatment for radiation exposure
segments.summary: Treatments include washing off contamination, Prussian blue for caesium and thallium, DTPA for plutonium, infection prevention, blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants.

segments.title: Abandoned places tangent
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss abandoned structures and the Grossinger's resort in New Jersey.

segments.title: Listener mail on physician suicide
segments.summary: A fourth-year medical student writes about suicide among doctors and medical students and promotes the documentary Do No Harm.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and point listeners to social media and the website.
